lead: >-
  The South Shetland Islands are an Antarctic archipelago north of the Antarctic Peninsula. Penguin colonies, glaciers, volcanic landscapes and research stations can all be found here. An expedition may visit several different islands, but actual landings depend on the itinerary, weather and environmental regulations.
---

## South Shetland Islands: location and highlights

The South Shetland Islands archipelago lies in the Southern Ocean north of the Antarctic Peninsula, separated from it by Bransfield Strait. This is one of the regions explored on Antarctic expeditions. Its landscapes include ice caps, cliffs, rocky shores, sheltered coves and coastlines with seabird colonies.

Rather than offering a single large island, the archipelago brings together distinctly different landscapes. King George Island has extensive research infrastructure; Deception Island bears clear signs of volcanic origins; glaciers and protected natural areas dominate elsewhere. That is why a cruise itinerary mentioning the “South Shetland Islands” needs closer examination: **which specific islands and bays** are actually planned?

The South Shetlands are geographically part of [Antarctica](/antarctica/) and lie within the Antarctic Treaty area. Visiting them is different from travelling to ordinary islands: special regulations apply to landings and entry into protected areas.

## The main islands and how they differ

### King George Island: researchers, stations and access from the mainland

[King George Island](/antarctica/place/king-george-island/) is the largest of the South Shetland Islands. It accommodates research and support facilities operated by several countries. Well-known locations include the [Chinese Great Wall Station](/antarctica/place/great-wall-station/), [Bellingshausen Station](/antarctica/place/bellingshausen-station/) and the Chilean settlement of [Villa Las Estrellas](/antarctica/place/villa-las-estrellas/).

The island's natural attractions are equally compelling. Potential stops include [Ardley Island](/antarctica/place/ardley-island/), with its penguin colonies, and [Collins Glacier](/antarctica/place/collins-glacier/). None of these stops, however, should be assumed to be included in every King George Island trip: access depends on permissions, weather and the chosen programme.

### Deception Island: an island with a volcanic caldera

Deception Island is a volcanic island in the archipelago. Its seawater-flooded caldera forms a natural harbour entered by ships through a narrow passage. Dark volcanic rock contrasts with snowy slopes and the sea.

Eruptions damaged operating stations during the twentieth century; the British Antarctic Survey documents volcanic events between 1967 and 1970. Deception Island is therefore interesting for both its geology and the history of scientific activity. Some areas are subject to environmental restrictions. A cruise visit to Deception Island must be checked against the vessel's actual itinerary.

### Livingston and other islands

Livingston, Ardley and other islands illustrate the variety of coastal environments across the archipelago. Some shores are dominated by glaciers, while others have exposed rock and seabird colonies. Travellers may observe these landscapes from the deck and, when conditions permit, go ashore in expedition boats.

When comparing itineraries, it is more useful to consider **how long the ship stays near the islands and what activities are planned** than simply to count the islands mentioned in a brochure. Sailing past an island and landing on it are different experiences with different weather requirements.

## Penguins, seals and whales: what you might see

The South Shetland Islands are home to chinstrap, gentoo and Adélie penguins, with different species found along different parts of the coast. Seabirds, seals and other polar wildlife also inhabit the region. Whales may be spotted in surrounding waters during expeditions, but sightings depend on the season, location and natural animal behaviour.

Wildlife encounters are managed so that animals are not disturbed. Visitors must not feed or touch birds and seals, approach nests or obstruct access routes to the sea. If an animal changes its behaviour because of human presence, visitors must increase their distance. Expedition staff determine permitted walking routes in accordance with these rules.

Even in the right season, no particular species can be guaranteed. If penguins, seals and whales are your main interest, compare [wildlife-focused journeys](/interests/wildlife/) and the geography of each itinerary. For glaciers and volcanic landscapes, explore the [Nature section](/interests/nature/).

## Expedition cruises and island landings

Most visitors discover the South Shetlands on an [Antarctic expedition cruise](/interests/cruises-and-expeditions/). Ships navigate between the islands, with shore landings made by small Zodiac boats when conditions allow. Cruises do not all visit the same places, and not every planned landing can go ahead.

Wind, waves, coastal surf and ice conditions are the main factors affecting landings. Restrictions may also arise from sensitive bird colonies, scientific work or an area's protected status. Expedition plans therefore remain flexible: an inaccessible landing may be replaced by observation from a boat or ship's deck, if conditions permit.

Ada Tours also offers another way to experience King George Island: an [overnight programme with a flight from Punta Arenas](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-overnight-program/). It focuses on specific places on the island, including research stations and a glacier. It is not equivalent to a multi-day cruise around the archipelago: the transport, places visited and allocation of time differ.

## When to go and what to pack

Expedition journeys to this region generally take place during the Southern Hemisphere summer. Polar summer does not mean warm weather. Wind, rain, snow and cold sea spray are possible even during a short coastal walk. Boat outings require warm layers, waterproof outerwear and footwear that meets the expedition operator's requirements.

Ask in advance about cleaning clothing and footwear before landings to avoid introducing foreign seeds and microorganisms into Antarctica. Collecting rocks, bones, plants or other natural objects is prohibited. Additional restrictions apply at research stations and in protected areas.

To choose an itinerary, consult the [catalogue of available Antarctica tours](/antarctica/tour/) and compare specific dates, days spent in Antarctic waters, transportation and planned stops.

## Frequently asked questions about the South Shetland Islands

### Are the South Shetland Islands part of Antarctica?

Yes. They are an Antarctic archipelago north of the Antarctic Peninsula, within the area covered by the Antarctic Treaty.

### Can I visit several islands on one cruise?

Yes, if the itinerary includes them and weather conditions permit. Visiting the region does not guarantee a landing on every island.

### Where are the Antarctic research stations located?

Many well-known stations are on [King George Island](/antarctica/place/king-george-island/). Access to individual research facilities requires prior approval.

### When can I see penguins and whales?

Different wildlife species may be encountered during the Southern Hemisphere summer expedition season, but their presence depends on the particular area and month. No expedition can guarantee a sighting of any specific animal.

lead: >-

On the 13-day voyage from Ushuaia, the expedition team selects observation points and landing sites according to weather, sea and ice conditions. Here we explain how this possibility differs from programmes that include the archipelago in their main route, and how to prepare for different decisions by the captain.
---

## The South Shetland Islands as a possible expedition stop

The main destination of the [13-day “Antarctica: Beyond the Antarctic Circle” expedition](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-polar-circle-deep-south-13-days/) is the [Antarctic Peninsula](/antarctica/place/antarctic-peninsula/) and the journey south towards the Antarctic Circle. The [South Shetland Islands](/antarctica/place/south-shetland-islands/) feature in the programme's wider geographical scope. This means individual places in the archipelago may become part of the actual itinerary if conditions are suitable, but no particular landing is promised in advance.

Here you will find {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}} that may include a visit to the archipelago at the expedition team's discretion. This designation **does not automatically mean a separately charged excursion**. The expedition in question lists possible stops within its sea voyage; any separately priced optional activities must be distinguished from the possibility of a landing itself.

## How the 13-day voyage works

The expedition begins in [Ushuaia](/argentina/place/ushuaia/). After sailing through the Beagle Channel, the ship crosses the [Drake Passage](/antarctica/place/drake-passage/). Days 4–10 focus on the southern Antarctic Peninsula, its bays and islands, and progress towards the polar circle. The itinerary concludes with a return sea crossing.

Possible stops include areas near [Livingston Island](/antarctica/place/livingston-island/), Deception Island and [Whalers Bay](/antarctica/place/whalers-bay/). Potential experiences include observing penguin colonies, elephant seals, birds and volcanic shores. **None of these places is assigned a guaranteed landing date or time.** If the ship continues south without entering a particular bay, the expedition's principal objective and planned time around the peninsula remain intact.

Crossing south of the Antarctic Circle is itself conditional on suitable ice conditions. Travellers choosing this route should be prepared for changes in the sequence of visits across several regions.

## What changes if the ship approaches the archipelago

The South Shetland Islands lie north of mainland Antarctica. Different islands offer different sights: rocky shores with penguins, glaciers, research stations and evidence of volcanic activity.

Possible experiences depend on the specific location:

- [Livingston Island](/antarctica/place/livingston-island/) and the Hannah Point area are known for penguin colonies, seabirds and elephant seal haul-outs.
- [Deception Island](/antarctica/place/deception-island/) has a flooded volcanic caldera and dark shores.
- [Whalers Bay](/antarctica/place/whalers-bay/) offers a chance to see the remains of a whaling station, provided a landing is both permitted and safe.

A sightseeing trip by Zodiac may be possible instead of going ashore. The decision depends on sea conditions, wind, ice and applicable visitor regulations. References to animals describe the region's wildlife potential; they do not guarantee encounters with particular species.

## When to choose a tour with the islands on its main route

If exploring the South Shetland Islands is your main objective, compare [tours that include the archipelago on their principal route](/antarctica/place/south-shetland-islands/tour/). These include both sea expeditions from Ushuaia and air-cruises via King George Island. They differ in duration, the direction of flight and sea segments, and the time available to explore the islands.

This is an important distinction among our itineraries: **a “main route destination” still does not guarantee a specific landing**, although the journey is centred on the archipelago. “Can be added” denotes a wider range of possible activities subject to expedition conditions. Choose according to your priority: the islands, mainland bays or travelling far to the south.

## Preparing for a possible landing

Clothing for Zodiac trips and shore walks must protect you from wind, spray and wet snow. Follow the crew's briefing on boarding boats, cleaning footwear and equipment, and permitted paths ashore. Touching wildlife or disturbing colonies is prohibited in Antarctica, and entry to research facilities requires separate permission.

Consider in advance which parts of the expedition matter most to you and how flexible you can be about the visiting order. We can help compare the actual itinerary conditions with the experiences you are hoping for, so your expectations match the nature of polar expedition travel.

## Frequently asked questions about possible island visits

### Is a landing on the South Shetland Islands guaranteed?

No. In the 13-day expedition, individual islands are listed as possible destinations for days 4–10. The onboard team selects the exact locations according to navigation conditions.

### Is there an extra charge for visiting the archipelago?

An itinerary appearing under “Can be added” does not itself establish a surcharge. The programme describes potential stops within the expedition. Pricing for genuinely additional activities is determined by the terms of the chosen product.

### Can I visit the islands and cross the Antarctic Circle on the same tour?

Both objectives are included in the concept of the [13-day programme](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-polar-circle-deep-south-13-days/), but the actual route depends on weather and ice. Treat both as expedition possibilities rather than fixed stops.

### Where can I compare tours focused specifically on the archipelago?

See the [catalogue of main-route tours through the South Shetland Islands](/antarctica/place/south-shetland-islands/tour/). It lets you compare sea passages and air-cruises against their actual itineraries.

## Tours to the South Shetland Islands: where Antarctica begins

The South Shetland Islands lie north of the Antarctic Peninsula, across Bransfield Strait. The archipelago looks relatively compact on a map, but for expedition travellers it encompasses remarkably diverse places: glaciated coasts, islands with penguin colonies, research stations and the volcanic landscapes of Deception Island.

Our collection features {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}} whose main routes include the archipelago. For more about the region itself, see the [South Shetland Islands page](/antarctica/place/south-shetland-islands/). Choose how you want to arrive, compare the number of days and find out which visits are scheduled and which are subject to the expedition team's decisions.

| Programme | Main feature |
|---|---|
| [“Antarctica Express”, 6 days](/multi-country/tour/antarctica-patagonia-express-air-cruise-6-days/) | Ship outbound, flight back |
| [“Classic Antarctica”, 8 days](/antarctica/tour/classic-antarctica-air-cruise-8-days/) | Flight and expedition ship |
| [“Discovery and Learning”, 11 days](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-discovery-learning-11-days/) | Sea passages and wildlife observation |
| [“Discovery and Long Hikes”, 11 days](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-discovery-long-hikes-11-days/) | Expedition with hiking options |

**The number of days does not determine how many landings you will make on the archipelago.** Compare the start and finish of the route, time aboard, daily activities and conditions for possible landings.

## Air-cruise or sea crossing of the Drake Passage

The [6-day “Antarctica Express” programme](/multi-country/tour/antarctica-patagonia-express-air-cruise-6-days/) begins in Argentina's [Ushuaia](/argentina/place/ushuaia/). The ship travels through the Beagle Channel and around Cape Horn, then crosses the [Drake Passage](/antarctica/place/drake-passage/) towards the South Shetland Islands. At the end, travellers arrive on [King George Island](/antarctica/place/king-george-island/) and fly to Punta Arenas in Chile. This reduces the return sea journey, but **does not eliminate the Drake Passage crossing on the way to Antarctica**.

The [8-day “Classic Antarctica” air-cruise](/antarctica/tour/classic-antarctica-air-cruise-8-days/) begins in Punta Arenas. A flight to King George Island is scheduled for day 2. After landing, the group walks approximately 2 km through the area of Frei and Bellingshausen stations and boards an expedition vessel using a Zodiac boat. The ship then explores the waters between the South Shetland Islands and the western Antarctic Peninsula. **The key difference** is that an air segment replaces the usual two-day outbound sea crossing from Ushuaia to the Antarctic islands.

Both programmes depend in part on air transport. Flights are weather-dependent, and an expedition does not operate like a city tour with a fixed timetable. If avoiding long periods on the open sea is a priority, compare these two journeys by the actual direction of their sea and flight segments, not merely by the term “air-cruise”.

## Two 11-day itineraries: how the island programmes differ

[“Antarctica: Discovery and Learning”](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-discovery-learning-11-days/) and [“Antarctica: Discovery and Long Hikes”](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-discovery-long-hikes-11-days/) both depart from Ushuaia. Each includes a crossing of the Drake Passage, time around the Antarctic Peninsula and the South Shetland Islands, and a return voyage by sea. Both suit travellers comfortable spending a substantial part of their trip aboard an expedition ship.

The educational programme focuses on observing nature, seabirds, penguins and glacial landscapes. The long-hikes version places greater emphasis on walking: conditions permitting, snowshoe outings near Damoy Point and hiking on a volcanic island may be offered. These are **optional expedition activities**, not guaranteed hikes along a specific trail at a fixed time.

Both 11-day programmes allocate **day 8 to the South Shetland Islands**. One possible destination is Deception Island, where the narrow Neptune's Bellows passage leads into a flooded volcanic caldera. The remains of a whaling station can be found at Whalers Bay. Even when a particular place appears in the day's description, whether a landing goes ahead is decided by the captain and expedition guides in light of sea conditions, wind and local restrictions.

When choosing between these 11-day journeys, first decide what matters more: **learning about nature and polar research** or the opportunity for longer activities ashore. Hiking options do not mean that every guest must complete a strenuous trek; individual limitations should be considered alongside the specific conditions of the chosen programme.

## What you can see in the archipelago

The islands offer several distinct experiences. King George Island hosts research stations operated by different countries and an airfield used for certain air-cruises. It provides insight into the organisation of scientific work in polar latitudes. At the same time, **a research station appearing on an itinerary does not mean visitors can enter freely**: visits require the station's agreement and must follow its rules.

Deception Island is altogether different. It is an active volcanic system with a flooded caldera that ships may enter through a narrow passage. Its geology has produced black volcanic slopes and a natural harbour. The British Antarctic Survey records eruptions in the latter half of the twentieth century that led to the abandonment of some stations. This makes the island appealing to those interested in both active geology and the history of polar expeditions.

Elsewhere in the archipelago, penguin colonies, seabirds, seals and glacial bays are among the main attractions. Wildlife sightings depend on the season and the animals' natural behaviour, not on promises of a particular photograph. For itineraries with this emphasis, see the [Antarctica wildlife tours catalogue](/interests/wildlife/tours/antarctica/); the broader range of expedition formats appears under [Antarctica cruises and expeditions](/interests/cruises-and-expeditions/tours/antarctica/).

## Preparing for landings and why routes can change

Landings from expedition vessels usually take place in small groups using Zodiac boats, if included in the programme and if conditions permit. Wind, surf, ice, protected-area restrictions and shore conditions may alter a landing site or prevent going ashore altogether. It is therefore better to judge a trip by its **complete expedition itinerary** rather than a guarantee of visiting one particular bay.

The main rules for visitors to Antarctica concern safety and conservation. Ashore, follow the guide's instructions, remain on permitted routes, avoid touching wildlife and leave natural objects where they are. Clothing and footwear are cleaned before boarding and after returning to remove possible contaminants and seeds. These measures form part of the responsible visitor guidelines published by the Antarctic Treaty Secretariat and IAATO.

Personal essentials include waterproof outer layers, wind protection, slip-resistant footwear and clothing that can be layered for warmth. Equipment provided aboard varies between programmes: check the exact “included” list for your chosen tour. There is no universal promise of identical boots, jackets or hiking routes on all departures.

## Choosing the right itinerary

If time is limited, consider the [6-day “Antarctica Express”](/multi-country/tour/antarctica-patagonia-express-air-cruise-6-days/), remembering that it includes a Drake Passage sea crossing. If approaching the archipelago by air before exploring by ship appeals more, compare the [8-day “Classic Antarctica”](/antarctica/tour/classic-antarctica-air-cruise-8-days/). For a longer sea expedition, look at the [11-day “Discovery and Learning”](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-discovery-learning-11-days/) or the [long-hikes version](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-discovery-long-hikes-11-days/).

If your priority is travelling as far south as possible, also compare the [expedition beyond the Antarctic Circle](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-polar-circle-deep-south-13-days/). It has a different objective: the South Shetland Islands are part of its extended possible geography, while its main focus is the Antarctic Peninsula and a potential voyage beyond the circle. This should not be confused with an itinerary centred on the archipelago.

## Frequently asked questions about South Shetland Islands tours

### Can I fly to the islands?

Yes. Some air-cruises use the airfield on King George Island. For example, [“Classic Antarctica”](/antarctica/tour/classic-antarctica-air-cruise-8-days/) includes a flight from Punta Arenas. Other voyages cross the Drake Passage by ship first. Always check the arrival arrangements for each tour.

### Is a visit to Deception Island guaranteed?

No. In the 11-day expeditions, Deception Island is described as a possible landing site in the South Shetland Islands. The decision depends on weather, ice, safety and visitor restrictions. The exact location is determined during the expedition.

### How do the South Shetland Islands differ from the Antarctic Peninsula?

They are an archipelago north of the peninsula, separated by Bransfield Strait. The islands are known for bird colonies, volcanic scenery and research stations, while the peninsula offers different channels, glaciers and bays. Many cruises cover both regions, but their reach towards southern destinations and the time spent there vary.

### Is this trip suitable for people who do not want long hikes?

Yes. Some expeditions emphasise observation from the ship and shorter outings when the shore is accessible. Compare the [8-day air-cruise](/antarctica/tour/classic-antarctica-air-cruise-8-days/) and the [11-day educational expedition](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-discovery-learning-11-days/). However, boarding a Zodiac, walking on uneven ground and coping with changing weather may demand physical stability, so check the specific limitations and assistance available for landings on your chosen programme.

  Villa Las Estrellas is a Chilean settlement on King George Island in Antarctica. Part of the infrastructure of Presidente Frei Air Base, it offers a glimpse of daily life among the polar ice. Visits are possible as part of an approved programme and depend on the weather.
---

## What is Villa Las Estrellas in Antarctica?

Villa Las Estrellas (“Village of the Stars”) is situated on [King George Island](/antarctica/place/king-george-island/), the largest island in the [South Shetland Islands](/antarctica/place/south-shetland-islands/) archipelago. It is a Chilean settlement within the Presidente Eduardo Frei Montalva Air Base complex. Residential buildings and support facilities stand near working areas, while rocky shores and Antarctic landscapes begin beyond the settlement.

Unlike penguin colonies and glaciers, the main interest of Villa Las Estrellas lies in human life. The settlement offers a sense of the challenges people face far from the mainland: keeping heating, electricity, communications, water supplies and essential deliveries working through strong winds and long winters.

## How the settlement developed

The Chilean Air Force dates the founding of Villa Las Estrellas to **1984**. The settlement grew alongside the operating base on King George Island. At different times it has accommodated polar infrastructure workers and their families.

Today the site remains part of the Presidente Frei complex. In 2025, the Chilean Air Force reported renovations of residential buildings, replacement of engineering systems and improvements to thermal insulation. This matters because the settlement belongs to a functioning base rather than an abandoned tourist attraction. Historical population figures and family numbers should not automatically be treated as current.

Villa Las Estrellas is also an example of civilian life under Antarctic conditions. Technical solutions become an everyday necessity here: even routine maintenance of a house depends on the delivery of materials, the weather and transport availability.

## What visitors can see

The main attraction is the combination of a polar settlement, service buildings and the stark surrounding landscape. During an approved stop, visitors may see the outside of the settlement, learn about air-base operations and observe how closely the facilities needed for life and scientific work are grouped together.

**Villa Las Estrellas is not a village where tourists have unrestricted access to every building.** Entering premises, visiting individual facilities or speaking with staff requires permission. Even a short guided walk through authorised areas can be rewarding, especially when a guide explains the history of human activity on the island.

King George Island offers many other places of interest. [Bellingshausen Station](/antarctica/place/bellingshausen-station/) illustrates Russia's scientific presence, while [Great Wall Station](/antarctica/place/great-wall-station/) reflects the history of Chinese research. The island's natural sights provide another perspective: birds may be observed near [Ardley Island](/antarctica/place/ardley-island/), while [Collins Glacier](/antarctica/place/collins-glacier/) showcases the island's glacial scenery. Access to each place is assessed separately.

## Getting to Villa Las Estrellas

The route depends on the format of your [Antarctica journey](/antarctica/). The [Ada Tours overnight programme](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-overnight-program/) includes a flight from Punta Arenas in Chile to King George Island. Villa Las Estrellas is scheduled for the first day alongside other sites. Further excursions and an overnight stay in an ice camp follow.

This is a specific fly-in itinerary and should not be confused with expedition cruises departing from Ushuaia. A cruise ship may visit other parts of the South Shetland Islands without calling at the Chilean settlement. When choosing a journey, check the day-by-day stops rather than relying only on the word “Antarctica” in a tour title.

Weather remains decisive even with air access. Strong winds and other conditions may affect flights, landings and the sequence of excursions. The Antarctic portion of an Ada Tours journey is subject to the weather.

## Preparing to visit the settlement

A short walk on the island calls for warm layered clothing with protection against wind and moisture. Check footwear and landing arrangements with the organiser: requirements for walking near the settlement may differ from those for a Zodiac landing.

At the operating base, follow your escorts' instructions, remain on permitted routes and avoid interfering with staff. International guidance for visitors to Antarctica prohibits disruption of scientific work and damage to natural features. It is worth establishing in advance whether the programme includes only an outside sightseeing stop or entry to specifically authorised interiors, as this significantly affects what you can expect.

## Frequently asked questions about Villa Las Estrellas

### Which island is Villa Las Estrellas on?

King George Island in the South Shetland Islands, north of the Antarctic Peninsula.

### Is it a research station or a town?

It is a small Chilean settlement within the infrastructure of the Presidente Frei Antarctic air base. Nearby scientific stations have their own functions and access regulations.

### Do people live here year-round?

The settlement is attached to an operating base and has residential facilities. Staffing changes, so older figures on residents and families cannot be presented as current statistics without further verification.

### Can I visit on a tour?

Yes. The settlement appears in the [Ada Tours overnight programme on King George Island](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-overnight-program/). Actual access and the order of visits depend on permissions and weather.

## Tours through Villa Las Estrellas: what you will see

On [King George Island](/antarctica/place/king-george-island/) there is a place quite unlike the familiar photographs of Antarctica: residential and service buildings linked by roads across rocky slopes and a rugged coastline. This is Villa Las Estrellas, a Chilean settlement in the [South Shetland Islands](/antarctica/place/south-shetland-islands/) archipelago.

Our selection includes {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}} with Villa Las Estrellas on their main route. They share the idea of discovering, in a single trip, life in a polar settlement, the activities of research stations and the island's natural landscapes. The main differences concern duration and accommodation.

**Visiting the settlement and sleeping on the island are not the same thing.** Even if a tour is described as an overnight programme, you need to check the actual sleeping location. In two published Ada Tours itineraries, guests stay at an ice camp near Collins Glacier, while Villa Las Estrellas is a sightseeing stop.

| Programme | Format |
|---|---|
| [Full-day tour from Punta Arenas](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-day-tour-from-punta-arenas/) | Fly in and return the same day |
| [Overnight Antarctica adventure](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-overnight-adventure/) | 1 night at an ice camp |
| [Overnight programme](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-overnight-program/) | Package with accommodation in Punta Arenas and 1 night on the island |

For more about the settlement, see the [dedicated Villa Las Estrellas page](/antarctica/place/villa-las-estrellas/). Here you can compare the available journeys.

## Day flight: a full experience without an overnight stay in Antarctica

The [full-day Antarctica tour from Punta Arenas](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-day-tour-from-punta-arenas/) is suitable for travellers who want to see King George Island and return to Chile without staying in a field camp in Antarctica.

The journey begins in Punta Arenas. A mandatory briefing is scheduled before departure: participants must reach the city the previous day, before 17:00, because attending the briefing is a condition of being admitted to the flight. In the morning the group is transferred to the airport and flies to King George Island.

On arrival, an approximately **5-hour programme on the island** is planned, including:
- an introduction to the Chilean settlement of Villa Las Estrellas;
- a visit to the area of the Russian Orthodox church near [Bellingshausen Station](/antarctica/place/bellingshausen-station/);
- a Zodiac outing towards [Ardley Island](/antarctica/place/ardley-island/) and penguin habitats;
- a boat trip towards [Collins Glacier](/antarctica/place/collins-glacier/).

A return flight to Punta Arenas is then planned, weather permitting. With several different sites on the itinerary, **time spent in the settlement itself is only part of the overall day**. The programme does not provide grounds for promising a long independent stroll among the houses or access to building interiors.

One important detail should be clarified when choosing this package: the published hotel-accommodation description lists 4 nights in Punta Arenas, while the structured tour duration is shown as 2 days and 1 night. ## Why life on King George Island is fascinating

King George Island is among the best-known South Shetland Islands. In a relatively small area, scientific and logistics facilities operated by several countries work alongside an airfield used by some expedition itineraries.

Villa Las Estrellas offers a rare opportunity to see the everyday infrastructure of a polar region. For visitors, it is quite different from watching icebergs from a ship or walking near a penguin colony. The interest lies in the practical realities of maintaining a settlement far from major cities: delivery of supplies, building maintenance, scientific activity and the dependence of travel on the weather.

Nearby facilities add to this story. [Bellingshausen Station](/antarctica/place/bellingshausen-station/) is connected with Russian scientific activity, while [Great Wall Station](/antarctica/place/great-wall-station/) represents China's presence. Research stations are workplaces, however: **being mentioned in an excursion does not automatically grant entry to laboratories or residential buildings**. Any visit must comply with the station's rules and availability.

The natural environment is equally significant. [Ardley Island](/antarctica/place/ardley-island/) attracts attention for its penguin colonies and coastal wildlife, while the [Collins Glacier](/antarctica/place/collins-glacier/) area illustrates the glaciated surroundings of King George Island. The combination of settlement, polar bases and natural sights sets these short trips apart from multi-day cruises along the Antarctic Peninsula.

## How the flight from Punta Arenas works

All three programmes depart from the Chilean city of Punta Arenas. The flight to Antarctica passes above southern Patagonia and the waters of the Drake Passage. After landing, the excursion continues on land and, where included, by boat.

This differs from a sea expedition departing from Ushuaia. There is no need for the usual multi-day ship crossing of the [Drake Passage](/antarctica/place/drake-passage/), but much depends on whether the flight can take place on the planned weather day. A delayed departure can shift the settlement visit and the excursions to Ardley or the glacier.

**Air travel does not guarantee an exact excursion start time.** Weather affects take-off, landing, travel around the island and boat outings. Ada Tours itineraries expressly state that the order of visits may change. If this journey is part of a longer holiday with onward international flights, it is prudent to allow extra time in Punta Arenas and review the change policy for the specific package.

The pre-flight briefing is equally important. Find out its requirements, location and arrival deadline when selecting the programme, rather than after buying your flights to Chile.

## What to wear and how to behave at research facilities

Even a short outing on King George Island calls for protection against wind, damp and rapidly changing conditions. Bring several warm layers, waterproof outerwear, gloves and suitable footwear. Check which boots, life jackets and other equipment are provided by the operator for your particular trip.

During Zodiac outings, follow the crew's and guide's instructions. Keep your distance from penguins and other wildlife, and do not attempt to provoke a reaction for a photograph. At scientific facilities, entering buildings without permission, touching equipment or collecting rocks and other natural objects is prohibited. Such rules protect both research areas and local nature.

If your programme includes a night near Collins Glacier, consider the camp's practical living conditions separately. Published itineraries refer to insulated tent modules, but this is **field accommodation**, not a standard hotel room. Before selecting a package, check suitable capacity, sleeping arrangements, toilet facilities, meals and restrictions relating to health and physical activity.

The same flexibility applies to additional island excursions: planned visits may be adjusted in response to the weather. Choose an Antarctic journey for the overall combination of experiences rather than relying on every individual stop taking place exactly as written.

## Frequently asked questions about tours through Villa Las Estrellas

### Can I visit Villa Las Estrellas in one day?

Yes. On the [day trip from Punta Arenas](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-day-tour-from-punta-arenas/), the settlement is part of a King George Island excursion. The overall land and boat programme lasts approximately 5 hours; the exact time spent in the settlement is not specified separately.

### Where do guests stay on the overnight programmes?

On the published [2-day](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-overnight-adventure/) and [5-day](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-overnight-program/) programmes, one night is spent at a special ice camp near Collins Glacier. The settlement itself is not listed as tourist accommodation.

### Can visitors enter Antarctic research stations?

Only when access has been explicitly agreed and authorised by the facility. Even where an itinerary mentions [Bellingshausen Station](/antarctica/place/bellingshausen-station/) or [Great Wall Station](/antarctica/place/great-wall-station/), this alone does not establish access to any interior rooms.

### Do all programmes include an excursion to see penguins?

All three tour descriptions include a boat outing towards [Ardley Island](/antarctica/place/ardley-island/) and its penguin colony. However, the ability to go out and observe wildlife depends on weather and natural conditions. Encounters are governed by Antarctic visitor regulations.

### Which programme should I choose if Villa Las Estrellas is my main interest?

First compare the length of the sightseeing stop and the full day's activities. All three published options combine the settlement with other sites on King George Island. If you want an extended visit focused specifically on life in the settlement, this needs to be arranged separately: none of the programmes described promises a standalone multi-hour tour exclusively of Villa Las Estrellas.
